title: The raft again (section 6)
hook: even the teaching is to be let go of, like a raft, and how much more what isn't the teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday, not seen by marks: wherever there are marks, there is illusion. Your line: beyond the marks.

Subhuti has a practical worry. He has just heard that a Buddha can't be seen by his marks. So he asks what anyone who has explained something subtle to a skeptical friend might ask: in some later age, when people hear words like these, will anyone actually trust them? The Buddha says yes, there will be such people. Then he reaches for a picture this path has met before, in the older discourses: a raft, built for a river, and the question of what to do with it once you're across.
screen: `WILL ANYONE TRUST THIS?` → `YES, SAYS THE BUDDHA.` → `A RAFT, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the worry answered. In a later time, the Buddha says, there will be people who keep the precepts, and when they hear even a single line of this teaching, a clear trust will arise in them. Their roots of goodness, the sutra says, weren't planted with one Buddha only, but with countless Buddhas. Second, how they hold it. They don't grab hold of teachings, and they don't grab hold of the denial of teachings either. Clutching the teaching is one ditch; clutching the idea that nothing matters is the other. Third, the raft. That's why, the Buddha says, his teaching is to be understood as a raft. Even teachings are to be let go of, and how much more what isn't teaching. Fourth, the raft before this one. In the Pali discourses, in a sutta called the Water Snake, a man facing a great flood binds grass, sticks and branches into a raft and paddles across. On the far shore he wonders whether to hoist it onto his head and carry it with him, out of gratitude. No, the Buddha says. Leave it on the bank and go on. The teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to. The Diamond Sutra pushes that old raft one step further: even the teaching itself, even this sutra. Nobody throws the raft away in the middle of the river. You need it on the water. The letting go comes when it has done its work.
screen: `WILL ANYONE TRUST THIS?` · `NOT TEACHING, NOT ITS DENIAL.` · `EVEN THE TEACHING IS A RAFT.` · `DON'T CARRY IT ON YOUR HEAD.` · then, large: `FOR CROSSING, NOT FOR HOLDING.`

segments.voice: Find one rule you've carried a long time, something that once got you across a hard stretch: never ask for help, always be early, keep the peace at any price. Thank it, the way you might pat a raft that kept you dry, and ask: am I still on the river, or carrying this on my head? You don't have to decide; just set it on the bank for this sit, and breathe beside it.
The raft again. The teaching is a raft for crossing; even it is let go of, and how much more what isn't the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: even the raft. A raft is for the river, not the road. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many schools use the raft picture to say that the teachings are tools for awakening, to be used fully and not clung to.

it's in the Pali Water Snake sutta too, where the man leaves the raft on the far bank.

fork.setup: you built a raft from grass and branches and crossed the flood on it. now you're on the far shore. what do you do with the raft?
options: carry it on your head, out of gratitude.
leave it on the bank and walk on.
break it apart so it can't be used again.
fork.reveal: in the Water Snake sutta, the Buddha says leave it on the bank: the teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to. the Diamond Sutra adds: even the teaching.

original.note: Sanskrit: a teaching, and also a thing or phenomenon; the sutra says even dharmas are let go of, like a raft.

trapdoor: what you thought: the raft means religion doesn't matter.
what it means: the teaching is a raft. use it fully on the water; don't carry it on your head once you're across.
what a scholar hears: the Diamond Sutra takes up the raft of the Pali Water Snake sutta and extends it to the teaching itself, steering between clinging to teachings and clinging to their denial.
guess: the teaching is a raft, let go of once it has carried you across
the teaching is a raft you should carry with you for life
the teaching is a raft to throw away before you start

chat.says: If the Buddha's teaching is true, why would the sutra say to let go of it?
options: It's like a raft: you need it on the river, and you set it down once you're across.
Because the sutra says the teaching was never really useful, even on the river.
It means the teaching was only for people in the Buddha's own lifetime.
chat.meaning: The Buddha says his teaching is to be understood as a raft: needed for crossing, then let go of, not carried on your head.

Subhuti.meaning: the disciple who questions the Buddha in this sutra

precepts.meaning: the basic moral rules Buddhists undertake to keep

Pali.meaning: the language of the Theravada scriptures

sutta.meaning: Pali for a discourse of the Buddha

Water Snake.meaning: a Pali discourse where the Buddha tells the raft story

notes: Section numbering follows the common 32-section division of Kumarajiva's Chinese text.
All wording paraphrased (quoted: null). The sutra's 'last five hundred years' is left out under the claims rule; the voice says 'a later time'.
'Roots of goodness planted with countless Buddhas' paraphrases the sutra's statement; the Chinese specifies numbers of Buddhas, deliberately left unspecified here.
Hook says the path 'has met' the raft before, in the older discourses (the title says 'again'); confirm that an earlier day of the Buddhism path taught MN 22's raft.
Alagaddupama Sutta rendered as 'the Water Snake' sutta; Keeper may prefer another English title.
